passage: Thursday. Science class was so hard today! Mr Iyer's chair squeaked when he sat, and it sounded like a duck. My whole body wanted to laugh. Suraj looked at me and I nearly burst. I pressed my lips together, bit my cheek and looked at my shoes. My shoulders were shaking. I held on until the bell, and then ran outside and laughed and laughed until I got hiccups. Suraj did too. It's hard, holding it in, but I know that class is not the place to laugh loudly. I felt proud that I did it, but I was also dying to let go. 😄 — Naveen

qa.q: What did the chair sound like?
qa.a: It sounded like a duck.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling during science class, and how do you know?
qa.a: Naveen was amused and trying to hold it in, with shaking shoulders and a bitten cheek. Naveen also felt proud of that control.

qa.q: What could Naveen do to release the energy afterwards?
qa.a: Naveen can run and laugh outside at break, as before, or share the joke with Suraj once class is over.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel on catching Naveen's eye?
qa.a: Suraj looked at Naveen and probably felt the same urge to laugh, and their eye contact made it harder for both.

grounding: A child holds in laughter in class using self-control, then releases the energy afterwards.

passage: At the village school in Kotra, the Class 4 children sat in a row on the mat waiting for their turn to read from the big book. Zeenat was seventh in line. She hopped her fingers on her knee and watched the others, whispering the words with her lips. Tanuja, the teacher, saw her and smiled. When the boy before Zeenat stumbled over a word, she almost blurted out the answer, and pressed her hand to her mouth instead. She waited until Tanuja nodded, and then read the whole page in one go. After school she ran three times around the banyan tree, shouting, and Tanuja watched her from the door.

qa.q: What place in line was Zeenat?
qa.a: Zeenat was seventh in line.

qa.q: How was Zeenat feeling when she pressed her hand to her mouth, and why did she wait?
qa.a: She was eager, almost bursting to say the word when the boy stumbled, but she held back to wait for her own turn, which shows growing self-control.

qa.q: What could adults do to help children who have to wait a lot?
qa.a: They can give chances to move and release energy afterwards, like running around the tree, as Zeenat did.

qa.q: How might Tanuja see Zeenat's behaviour in class and afterwards?
qa.a: Tanuja sees a child using restraint during class and needing to run afterwards. Tanuja smiles while watching, so seems to understand.

grounding: A child waits for her turn and holds back an answer, using self-control, then needs to release energy afterwards.

passage:
During silent reading in the Madrid classroom, Alejandro turned round and made a fish face at Selin, lips pushed out, eyes crossed.
Selin pressed her lips together hard. Her shoulders shook. She bit the inside of her cheek and stared at page forty-two until the words swam. A tiny squeak escaped. The teacher looked up. Selin turned the page very seriously.
Alejandro did it again. Selin put her book in front of her face.
When the bell rang, she ran out to the yard, grabbed Alejandro by the sleeve, and they both exploded with laughter, bent double by the fence. She laughed until her stomach hurt. Then they raced each other to the goalposts and back twice.

qa.q: What page was Selin staring at?
qa.a: Page forty-two.

qa.q: What was Selin feeling while she bit the inside of her cheek?
qa.a: She felt very amused and wanted to laugh, but was working hard to hold it in because it was silent reading time.

qa.q: What made the restraint easier to keep up?
qa.a: Knowing the bell would come helped, and running out to laugh and race in the yard gave her a place to let all that energy out.

qa.q: How might the teacher have seen Selin turning the page so seriously?
qa.a: The teacher probably saw a quiet reader and didn't notice the laughter being held in, except for the tiny squeak.

grounding: A child holds in laughter during silent reading using self-control, then releases it in the yard afterwards.

passage:
At the school science fair, Yash stood in line behind five other children to ask Ankita about her solar oven. He had a question burning in his mouth: would it melt chocolate?
Ankita was explaining slowly to the judge. Yash hopped from foot to foot. He opened his mouth, then closed it again. He counted the tiles on the floor.
Finally it was his turn. "Will it melt chocolate?" he blurted.
Ankita grinned. "Yes! I tested it yesterday."
Yash beamed.
After the fair, the teacher sent everyone out to the field for ten minutes. Yash ran three laps, arms out like a plane, shouting "CHOCOLATE!" at the sky.

qa.q: What did Yash count while waiting?
qa.a: The tiles on the floor.

qa.q: How can you tell Yash felt eager and impatient while waiting his turn?
qa.a: He hopped from foot to foot, opened and closed his mouth, and counted tiles, which shows eager excitement he was holding back.

qa.q: Why was the teacher's choice to send everyone to the field helpful?
qa.a: After a long time of self-control, running gave children like Yash a safe way to let out their bottled-up energy.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt answering Yash's question?
qa.a: Ankita probably felt pleased and proud that someone was so excited about her solar oven.

grounding: At a science fair, a child waits his turn with visible self-control, then gets a chance to release energy afterwards.

passage:
At our Nani's prayer meeting, the pandit's microphone suddenly made a loud squeaky noise, like a duck. Everyone kept their faces serious.
I saw my brother Uday press his lips together so tight they went white. His shoulders shook. He stared hard at the flowers in front of Nani's photo and breathed through his nose. I don't know if he was trying not to laugh or trying not to cry. Maybe both.
He managed it all through the prayers.
Afterwards, he went straight out to the garden and I followed. He laughed so hard he had to hold the gate, and then he wiped his eyes and went quiet.
I sat on the step next to him till Mummy called us for food.
- Yamini

qa.q: What sound did the microphone make?
qa.a: A loud squeaky noise, like a duck.

qa.q: What might Uday have been feeling when his shoulders shook?
qa.a: He may have been amused by the squeak and struggling not to laugh, or sad and holding back tears at the prayer meeting; Yamini can't be sure, and it may have been both.

qa.q: What helped Uday after holding it in so long?
qa.a: Going out to the garden gave him a private place to let the laughter and feelings out, with his sibling quietly beside him.

qa.q: How did Yamini experience watching Uday?
qa.a: Yamini was watching closely and caring, unsure what he felt, and chose to follow him and sit with him.

grounding: An observer watches a brother hold in laughter during a solemn prayer meeting, then release it afterwards outside.

passage:
Monday: During Hindi dictation, Disha crossed her eyes at Avni. Avni snorted so loudly that Ms Rao stopped reading, and Avni had to stand at the back, red-faced.
Wednesday: Disha did it again during silent reading. Avni pressed both lips together, stared hard at the book and dug a thumbnail into one palm. Avni's shoulders shook, but not a sound came out. When the bell rang, the two of them raced to the neem tree and laughed until they got hiccups.
Friday: In the class quiz Avni knew every answer and wanted to shout them all out, but sat on both hands and waited for a turn. Afterwards, Ms Rao let the whole class run two laps of the ground. Avni ran fastest of all.

qa.q: What did Disha do to make Avni laugh?
qa.a: Disha crossed her eyes at Avni.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling on Wednesday while the shoulders shook?
qa.a: Avni felt amused and bursting with laughter, but held it in with pressed lips and a thumbnail in the palm.

qa.q: What helped Avni's self-control work?
qa.a: Having ways to hold it in, like pressed lips and sitting on hands, and a release afterwards at the neem tree and on the laps.

qa.q: How might Ms Rao see the laps after the quiz?
qa.a: Ms Rao seems to know that children who have held themselves back need a chance to let the energy out, so the laps are a relief as much as a reward.

grounding: It illustrates a child growing the skill of holding in laughter and waiting for a turn, with chances to release energy afterwards.
